cells.tense: Right now you're the one keeping something steady while the ground keeps shifting, and you can feel each adjustment as you make it.
cells.ask: Name one adjustment out loud to the person it touches, today, and let their answer land on it.
cells.core:
You're keeping a shape in place while everything around it moves, and you know you're doing it. You read what needs adding, what needs subtracting, when to leave it alone — the small live sensing that keeps a thing whole. Nothing gets frozen. It gets re-found, again and again, and the people around you benefit from it without noticing.

What's missing is that no one else sees their part in it, or yours. Fair exchange isn't bookkeeping — it's letting something go out and come back changed. Tell one person about one adjustment you made today, and let what they say reach you.

cells.tense: You're already out past the end, trying to lock a shape that hasn't landed yet.
cells.ask: Leave one thing that's still forming alone for a day, and when the pull to step in shows up, note it and don't move.
cells.core:
You can feel this turning into a shape and your hands are already on it — adjusting something that hasn't finished arriving. Bracing like that costs more than it looks. At its plain best, a change is allowed to settle at its own pace while you stay close enough to catch what comes next.

The pull toward what might be felt is what you're chasing, and it feels urgent when it isn't. Let one unfinished thing stay unfinished for a day. When the urge to take hold of it shows up, write it down and wait — what comes back often tells you more than the taking would.

cells.tense: Something changed and you haven't let it be over, so you're still working on the version that finished.
cells.ask: Spend twenty minutes today doing the next actual task that a settled thing calls for, then check whether a direction has shown up.
cells.core:
Something has already happened and you're still holding the question open, which means nothing has a shape yet and the adjusting has nothing to move around. The feeling inside would tell you what to do and you'd follow it without much fuss — that's the easy version of this. As it stands, the inside signal is quiet, so you wait on the outside, and the outside says move, so nothing moves.

You don't get anywhere by pushing feeling into the quiet place. Pick one finished thing and give twenty minutes to what it actually asks you to do now. Direction tends to arrive once a thing is placed and you can feel it push back.

cells.tense: You're holding this steady by feel, adjusting as you go, and you'd call it drift rather than decide.
cells.ask: Say one sentence out loud today — to yourself, the notes on your phone, or one person — that names this as something you're keeping steady.
cells.core:
The steadying is already happening. You sense when to add, when to ease off, what to leave where it is, and it works — the thing holds because of it. What you describe is more like coasting, or just getting through, as though this ran without anyone at the wheel. The skill is real and it's been running quietly for a while.

Nothing changes until the doing gets put back in your hands. One plain sentence out loud, naming the thing as yours to keep steady, does it. The claim can be small, said once, and still change what you think you've been doing.

attempts.check: The verb and place lines are general enough to hold any life (kitchen-table, no images), so most of the risk is not in the card but in the seat's correction. The reader could fairly object that 'adjusting without forcing' is just being sensible; the cells name the specific cost — that the differentness gets kept quiet — so the ask still teaches something if the read is wrong. The sentence 'the differentness gets its energy back' is warm but could be read as the writer's flourish; it stays because it gives the act a plain finish.

attempts.check: The unsupported reach in my first pass was the seat line doing too much work ('the seat ran itself'), which is house vocabulary nobody at a table would say; the fix is to describe the same thing in plain words the person could answer back to. The reader could fairly say the asks are chores dressed up as insight; each one is a single visible act done today and each teaches something whether or not my read of them lands. The sentences that served the writer were the summary last lines — 'the holding is real,' 'that's the seat doing its work' — they get cut or rewritten so the cell closes on what the person gets, not on how the cell sounds.

attempts.check: The remaining refusal was a refrain I'd leaned on across cells; 'Right now the inside signal is quiet' gets rebuilt so the seat's emptiness is said once, in fresh words. The riskiest personal claim is in status 3 — that a finished thing is being held as an open question — which the card supports and which the ask doesn't depend on being true: if it's wrong, twenty minutes on the next real task still teaches the person what they actually want. The line I liked best for its own sound, 'you can feel it push back,' is the one a writer would keep; it earns its place or it goes, and here it does a job the reader can use.
